We are delighted to welcome Dr. Dhanshree Thulkar, PhD, PMP®, who joins IKP Knowledge Park as 𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗲𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿 – 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀.

Dr. Dhanshree brings over a decade of experience in AI-driven and deeptech programme management, technology translation and innovation ecosystems. Her expertise includes building strategic partnerships and fostering academia-industry collaborations. She holds a Ph.D. in Machine Learning and Healthcare AI Systems from Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute (VJTI) Mumbai, an M.Tech from Shri Guru Gobind Singhji Institute of Engineering and Technology, Vishnupuri, Nanded and a B.Tech from Nagpur University.

At IKP, she will lead strategic partnerships and resource mobilisation, focusing on identifying funding opportunities, building relationships with CSR organisations, government agencies and academic institutions, and securing grants and institutional partnerships to advance our programmes and initiatives.

Welcoming her to the team, IKP CEO Dr. Satya Prakash Dash said: "Dhanshree's experience in deeptech, technology translation and programme management will add valuable strength to our efforts to build meaningful collaborations with industry, government, academia and funding partners."

Please join us in extending a warm welcome to Dr. Dhanshree Thulkar and wishing her every success in her new role!

We hosted Prof. Hiroaki Kitano and Dr Ravindranath Kancherla for an engaging exchange on innovation, technology and opportunities for collaboration.

A pioneer in systems science and systems biology, Prof. Kitano has made significant contributions to advancing interdisciplinary research and technology. He has also served as Chief Technology Officer of Sony Group Corporation. Dr. Ravindranath is a healthcare pioneer, a world-renowned expert in Surgical Gastroenterology and Laparoscopic Surgery and Founder, Global University Foundation.

During their visit, the guests learned about about two of our key innovation platforms — 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁-𝗙𝗮𝗯, our manufacturing-as-a-service facility, our upcoming 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲 and our portfolio of innovative deep science startups across climate tech, medtech, biopharma. The discussions also explored potential avenues for future collaboration with IKP.

We look forward to building on these conversations and exploring opportunities to connect expertise, infrastructure and innovation to advance science and technology.

Every time India celebrates a semiconductor milestone, I think about 2021.

Car plants around the world stopped. The cause wasn't some advanced processor. It was small, cheap, boring chips, made in one country and sometimes in one plant. When that link broke, everything downstream broke with it.

India has put serious money into making sure that never happens to us again. Over ₹2 lakh crore across two programmes. Three plants already in commercial production. Our first chips are out.

So I don't think the question anymore is whether India will have a semiconductor industry. It will. The question I keep coming back to is where India becomes hard to replace.

Working with chip startups at SINE, I've come to believe the answer has less to do with design than we assume. We have the engineers. Our startups are taping out. What they struggle with is what comes after: getting someone to actually buy the chip, at volume, for years.

From the other side, the hesitation makes sense. An OEM that qualifies a new chip spends a year testing it and takes a bet on a supplier with no track record. A fab or packager would rather fill capacity with big foreign orders. Investors hold back because there are no customers yet. Everyone is waiting for someone else to go first.

A chip company needs a whole village behind it. Capital, customers and factories have to move together, because each one derisks the others. A purchase order makes a startup fundable. Funding makes it safe to buy from. Volume makes it worth a fab's time.

If adoption is the real constraint, India should play where adoption is easiest to win. They could be simple - analog, power and mixed signal chips for markets India already controls: smart meters, motors, EVs, CCTV. The buyers are Indian, the rules are Indian, and the chips use mature nodes our own fabs can make.

India won't be judged on whether it can make a chip. We've done that. It will be judged on whether a meter maker in Pune, a carmaker in Stuttgart and a packager in Sanand all say yes to the same Indian chip for ten years.

What does it take for an innovation to actually reach the people it was designed to serve?

Sometimes, the biggest barrier isn't the technology. It's everything that needs to happen around it.

During a field visit, a woman farmer in Hatipur handed over ₹10 to the team behind an initiative that had brought new technologies to her community. It wasn't a payment or charity, but a blessing, a reciprocal gesture of gratitude for the economic independence those innovations had helped create.

For Onkar Pandey, Director at Social Alpha, this is what meaningful impact looks like: solutions that respond to real needs and create value for the communities they are designed to serve.

In the second episode of Voices of Value, we draw on Onkar's more than two decades of experience in the development sector to explore what it takes to move agricultural innovations beyond research institutions and pilot projects and into the hands of farmers.

Our conversation looks at why promising technologies often struggle to scale, the role of financing, distribution and after-sales support, and how collaboration between farmers, governments and philanthropic institutions can help build the ecosystems needed for adoption.

Onkar also shares a simple but important piece of advice for early-stage social entrepreneurs:

“Solve the problem. Revenue will chase you.”

A perspective that puts the focus where it belongs: on understanding the problem, earning the trust of communities and building solutions that can sustain themselves over time.

For millions of smallholder farmers, climate change is not an abstract environmental challenge to debate at yet another conference or articulate in yet another report. It is an everyday economic reality. 

Unpredictable rainfall, water scarcity, declining soil health, rising input costs and uncertain crop yields directly affect household incomes and livelihood security. Women face additional disadvantages when technologies, productive assets and market opportunities are not designed around their needs.

These challenges are deeply interconnected. And so must be the solutions. 

This Lab to Land documentary series features six innovators working across soil health, water conservation, biological inputs, clean energy, agricultural mechanisation and sustainable farming. Each innovation approaches a different problem. But together, they illustrate something much larger.

𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱𝘀. 𝗦𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝘃𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻 𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘀, 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀.

And resilience is not simply the ability to survive the next shock. It is the capacity to become progressively less vulnerable while building greater economic opportunity. 

Entrepreneurship is about doing — taking risks, building solutions and demonstrating value. It can play a transformative role in building economic resilience, helping people improve their incomes, reduce costs, manage risks, adapt to climate change and build more secure livelihoods. But a technology must work reliably, demonstrate economic value, become affordable and accessible, and earn the trust of its users. For resource-constrained communities, experimenting with unproven technologies can be prohibitively risky. Someone must absorb those risks, validate solutions and help build the markets that make widespread adoption possible.

Our role is not simply to finance innovation. It is to help create the conditions in which innovation can succeed, markets can emerge, and impact can endure.

These six stories illustrate a larger proposition: economic prosperity, climate resilience, environmental sustainability and social inclusion need not be competing objectives. With the right innovations and institutions, they can reinforce one another.

The six-month programme offers selected eligible women-led micro and small enterprises support with:
- Business formalisation and registrations
- Financial readiness and credit linkages

The acceleration support is fully covered for selected eligible participants.

At the Gujarat Innovation and Technopreneurship (GInTech) Conclave 2026, organised by Savli Technology and Business Incubator (STBI), under the Department of Science & Technology, Government of Gujarat, at GIFT City Club, Gandhinagar, Avinash Punekar, CEO, iCreate, joined government representatives, industry leaders and startup ecosystem stakeholders to discuss advancing technology-led entrepreneurship.

A moment of national recognition for iCreate portfolio startups at the Bharat RE Summit & Expo 2026 in New Delhi.

Two iCreate portfolio startups, Apeiro Energy and Tectonic Power Pvt. Ltd., had the opportunity to interact with the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, and showcase their indigenous innovations contributing to India's renewable energy and clean technology landscape.

Kalpit Prajapati, Founder of Apeiro Energy, highlighted the startup's low-wind-speed vertical turbine technology, designed to explore new possibilities for harnessing wind energy along railway tracks and highways.

Dr. Khushbu Patel (Butani), Co-Founder & CTO of Tectonic Power, showcased the company's indigenously developed, patented PBI-based composite membrane technology, which combines agricultural waste-derived nano-silica with Polybenzimidazole (PBI) for applications in green hydrogen electrolysers and high-temperature PEM fuel cells.

These interactions reflect the growing capabilities of India's deep tech startup ecosystem and the role of homegrown innovations in advancing the country's clean energy ambitions.

At iCreate, we remain committed to nurturing innovators and supporting startups developing technologies for a more sustainable future.
